---
title: "About Me"
---

Seeds are small wonders that hold whole forests inside them. Understanding how they travel, survive and become trees has been the thread running through my career — from field plots in the Colombian Andes to international conservation programmes today.

I lead international tree seed conservation and forest restoration projects for the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, connecting scientific research with policy, funding and on-the-ground delivery to protect and restore threatened forests. As Latin America Projects Coordinator within the Millennium Seed Bank Partnership's Global Tree Seed Bank programme, I coordinate the design, implementation and partnership management of conservation projects across the region — currently restoring the natural capital of Mexican forests and developing seed-based solutions for threatened Magnolia forests in Mesoamerica and the Caribbean. I work directly with in-country research institutions, protected-area authorities, NGOs and local communities to turn seed science into conservation outcomes.

I am a seed ecologist with a doctorate (magna cum laude) from Goethe University Frankfurt and the Senckenberg Biodiversity and Climate Research Centre, and the author of peer-reviewed publications on seed ecology, dispersal and tropical forest regeneration.

Across more than a decade in Colombia, Ecuador, Spain, Germany and the UK, my work has centred on connecting knowledge, people and action: leading the production of bilingual seed guides with international partners, training restoration practitioners across Colombia as a GIZ diaspora expert, and contributing to national conservation policy. I work fluently across cultures, sectors and languages (native Spanish, professional English).

I am focused on strengthening the global networks that make forests — and the people who steward them — more resilient, and on building partnerships that deliver lasting impact for biodiversity conservation and restoration.
